messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Harald is a 76-year-old divorced man of European descent who has managed a mid-sized hotel in a mid-Atlantic city for the better part of two decades. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 73, seeking help approximately fourteen months after a toxic chemical exposure that occurred during a routine inspection of the hotel's basement utility corridor. A maintenance contractor had improperly stored and mixed industrial cleaning agents; when Harald opened the corridor door that morning, he was met with a dense, acrid cloud. He recalls the burning in his throat and eyes, the way his legs gave out, and the particular smell — sharp, synthetic, somehow sweet underneath — before losing consciousness. He was hospitalised for four days. Physically, he recovered. Psychologically, he has not.

In the weeks following discharge, Harald noticed that his memories of the event did not cohere into a narrative he could hold or examine. Instead, they arrived in disconnected pieces — the metallic taste, a fragment of fluorescent light, the sound of his own coughing — that surfaced without warning and without sequence. Most disorienting was the way the emotional intensity of those moments could flood him without any accompanying image: he would be standing at the hotel front desk and feel, without knowing why, the absolute certainty that he was dying. These intrusive memory fragments, arriving without context or resolution, began to shape how he understood what had happened to him. He had come to believe that his body could no longer be trusted — it had failed him without warning in a place he knew intimately — and that he was fundamentally helpless to prevent catastrophe from recurring. His body, he felt, had become something alien and unreliable, an enemy that kept reacting as though the danger were still present.

These appraisals deepened his sense of threat. Because he could not trust his own body to signal real danger accurately, he began treating the entire world as a potential source of harm. At home — a modest apartment he had retreated to more and more — he remained perpetually on guard, scanning rooms, checking locks, unable to settle. Unexpected sounds, the clatter of a dropped tray at the hotel or a car backfiring outside, sent his heart into his throat and his mind immediately back toward the basement corridor. The smell was the worst of it: certain cleaning products used by the hotel's housekeeping staff could summon, with horrible fidelity, the olfactory texture of that morning, and when that happened the threat Harald felt was no longer abstract. It was immediate, physical, and indistinguishable from the original.

The state of heightened threat, in turn, kept the memories close to the surface. The more vigilant he was, the more readily a fragment would break through — a sound, a smell, a flicker of fluorescent light in a conference room — and the cycle would tighten. To manage this, Harald developed a set of strategies that made sense to him at the time. He began keeping loud music or the television running constantly in his apartment, filling the acoustic space so that unexpected sounds had less room to register. He monitored his own thoughts with exhausting vigilance, scanning for signs that he was "losing his mind," as he put it — certain that if he caught a thought early enough, he could prevent a full intrusion. He had not returned to the basement corridor since the exposure, and he had quietly rearranged his management duties so that a junior colleague handled all utility and maintenance inspections.

These strategies, however, extracted their own costs. The constant noise and self-surveillance left Harald feeling more fragmented, not less, and he had come to see his need for them as further evidence that his body and mind were beyond his control. The avoidance had not gone unnoticed by his staff; his withdrawal from certain operational areas had created confusion and, eventually, a formal complaint about managerial inconsistency. He now feels safe only in a narrow circuit — his office, his apartment, a single café nearby — and the shrinking of that circuit has confirmed, in his mind, the very helplessness he fears.

What finally brought Harald to seek help was a conversation with his daughter, who lives abroad and noticed during a video call that he had lost considerable weight and had not left his apartment in nine days. What he most fears is that he will never recover his sense of competence or safety. What he most hopes is simply to be able to walk back into his own hotel without feeling that he is about to die.
